claims.text: The target material is a tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy similar to magnetron-sputtered quaternary W-Ta-V-Cr.
The cited W-Ta-V-Cr alloy is nanocrystalline.
Aluminum surface enrichment can create a diffusion zone capable of supplying aluminum for oxide formation.
Introducing a thin aluminum-enriched surface layer will promote in situ formation of an adherent Al2O3 scale on the tungsten-based alloy.
The resulting Al2O3 scale will be continuous and adherent.
Aluminum at the surface preferentially oxidizes because of its strong affinity for oxygen.
Preferential oxidation of surface aluminum produces thermodynamically stable alumina.
An alumina scale acts as a diffusion barrier that slows oxygen ingress into the substrate.
Slower oxygen ingress mitigates oxidation of the underlying alloy.
The aluminum-enriched alloy will have a significantly lower oxidation rate than the untreated alloy.
The aluminum-enriched alloy will develop a thinner oxide layer than the untreated alloy.
Reduced oxidation will improve structural stability at extreme temperature.
The untreated alloy is expected to form less protective and possibly nonuniform oxide layers.
The untreated alloy is expected to suffer more severe oxidation degradation over time.
The intervention should be effective at approximately 1000°C in air during a 50-hour exposure.
The proposed effective temperature range for protective alumina formation is roughly 900°C to 1200°C at oxygen partial pressures typical of air.
The efficacy of the intervention outside 900°C to 1200°C and air-like oxygen partial pressures is uncertain.
The beneficial effect of aluminum on oxidation resistance is well established in many alloy systems.
The optimal aluminum concentration profile and enriched-layer thickness for this nanocrystalline tungsten-based HEA are not established.
The effects of aluminum surface enrichment on bulk mechanical properties under irradiation and high-temperature conditions remain unresolved.
